title: Human stress responses in office-like environments with wood furniture
research_question: To determine if using wood furniture in offices could improve stress responses and recovery compared to control environments (offices without wood), by assessing stress indicators in different scenarios to understand the response more fully.

participants.description: 61 healthy adults (18-52 years, mean: 27.7 ±9.3 years; 47 female, 14 male) from Slovenia and Italy, including long-term visitors. Non-smokers, not taking prednisolone, without heart conditions exacerbated by stress, and without other stress-related conditions.
participants.recruitment: Through e-mail distributed to regional organizations and mailing lists, advertisements on local media, social networks, and in classrooms on campus at the University of Primorska.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Two adjacent office-like environments (A and B), each divided into two equal-sized portions (approx. 2.5m x 2.5m). Curtains blocked exterior windows. Each office had a control setting (white furniture, no visible wood) and a wood setting. Office A's wood setting had oak veneered furniture. Office B's wood setting had American walnut veneered furniture. Furniture included a desk, bookshelf, filing cabinet, and drawers.

Two segments of feature films (approx. 6 min each) featuring intense scenes of physical violence, shown on a tablet or laptop computer with volume on, to induce stress. Videos were randomized between tests, subjects did not see the same video twice.

findings.quote: There was no evidence of a within-subjects difference in WHO-5 well-being index scores between tests (paired, two-sided p-value: .30).

mechanisms: Wood furniture in the built environment may act as a passive environmental intervention to reduce physiological stress responses (cortisol).
The visual characteristics of different wood types (e.g., lighter oak vs. darker walnut) may differentially influence stress responses.
moderators: Lighting levels (though intended to be constant, visual brightness differed)
implementation_implications: Using wood furniture, particularly lighter-colored wood like oak, in office environments may be a useful, affordable, and readily available way to improve the health of office workers by reducing cortisol responses to stress.
When selecting wood furniture, visual characteristics (e.g., color, brightness) and their interaction with other indoor environment elements (e.g., lighting) should be considered.
Future studies should extend the test duration to at least 90 minutes and collect saliva samples more frequently during the recovery period to better observe stress recovery.
Future studies should maintain consistent luminance across test environments and include emotional/affective scales for more contextual information.

limitations: The duration of the test period (75 min) may have been too short to observe a greater degree of stress recovery.
Saliva samples were not collected with sufficient frequency in the later part of the test period to observe peak stress and stress recovery in greater detail.
Luminance levels were not maintained constant across all test environments, potentially confounding results due to differences in visual brightness between oak and walnut rooms.
The study did not include an emotional or affective scale, limiting contextual information about the stress response valence.
The stressor used may not have been strong enough to produce a robust effect, or the expected effect size was small, making detection of magnitude differences challenging.
The observed differences in cortisol concentrations were small, suggesting that the full impact on humans is cumulative rather than immediate.
